title: Generic types and methods (open types, closed types, inference)
hook: A generic type puts the type parameter on the class or struct. A generic method puts it on the method itself. You close types when you construct them, and the compiler usually infers method type arguments from what you pass in.

blocks.text: An open generic type still has an unbound type parameter — for example class CacheClient<T>. A closed generic type supplies a real type — CacheClient<SessionDto>. Generic methods work the same way: static void Print<T>(T value) is open; Print(42) closes T as int through type inference. You can nest generics: Dictionary<string, List<Message>>. Interfaces, structs, records, and delegates can all be generic.

entries.plainDefinition: A generic type or method that still has an unbound type parameter like T.
entries.example: List<T> is open; you cannot new List<T>() without supplying T.

entries.plainDefinition: A generic type or method where every type parameter has been replaced with a concrete type.
entries.example: List<string> is a closed generic constructed from List<T>.

entries.plainDefinition: The compiler deducing type arguments from method call arguments so you do not write them explicitly.
entries.example: Print(42) infers T as int without writing Print<int>(42).

blocks.text: Generic types let you build reusable components — caches, repositories, pipelines — without duplicating code per DTO. Static fields on a generic class are per closed type: CacheClient<int> and CacheClient<string> do not share the same static dictionary. That detail has bitten many "global stats" counters. Generic methods let you write one algorithm — GetOrAdd, Max, Parse — that works across types while constraints (covered in the next topic) tell the compiler what T can do.

blocks.title: When to use a generic type versus a generic method
blocks.body: Put T on the class when the whole object is about one type (RedisCache<T>). Put T on the method when only that operation needs it (Parse<T>(json)). Do not create a ten-parameter generic God-class — split responsibilities instead.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Declare an open generic
items.body: Write class Foo<T> or static void Bar<T>(T value). T is a placeholder.

items.title: Close the type at use site
items.body: new RedisCache<SessionDto>(db) binds T to SessionDto for that instance.

items.title: Call a generic method
items.body: Pass arguments; the compiler infers T from them. Print(42) → T is int.

items.title: Specify explicitly when inference fails
items.body: When T appears only in the return type, write Parse<Message>(json) because nothing in the arguments names T.

snippet.label: Generic type plus generic method
snippet.explanation: RedisCache<T> closes T at construction — one cache instance per value type. GetOrAdd is a generic method that infers TKey and TValue from the dictionary argument. The notnull constraint on TKey matches Dictionary's own requirement.

snippet.label: Static fields are per closed type
snippet.explanation: Counter<int> and Counter<string> each get their own static Count field. This is not one shared counter — a common interview trap.

snippet.label: Inference and explicit type arguments
snippet.explanation: Inference uses call arguments. When T only appears in the return type, you must write Empty<string>(). Collection expressions and target typing (C# 12+) can close generics from the left-hand side.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming static fields on Generic<T> are shared across all T — they are per closed type. Fighting inference instead of writing Foo<T>(...) explicitly when the compiler cannot deduce T. Putting T on the class when only one method needed it, creating unnecessary coupling.

blocks.text: An **open generic** still has an unbound type parameter — `List<>` in reflection via `typeof(List<>)`, or `RedisCache<T>` before you close T. A **closed generic** supplies concrete arguments — `List<string>`. You cannot `new List<>()` without closing T. Static members on generic types are keyed by the **closed type**: `Counter<int>.Count` is independent of `Counter<string>.Count`. At the JIT level, **generic sharing** means many closed types with reference-type arguments reuse the same native implementation; value-type closures get per-T code. Generic methods infer type arguments from call sites; when T appears only in the return type, you must specify `Empty<string>()`. How to prove it in production: log `typeof(RedisCache<>).GetGenericTypeDefinition()` in startup diagnostics; BenchmarkDotNet comparing static counter fields across two closed types.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Used in DI, reflection, factory patterns
Real constructed type; statics are per closure
T inferred or specified at call site
Reference T args often share JIT body
Value types get separate native code

snippet.label: Open generic reflection and closed construction
snippet.explanation: typeof(List<>) is the open generic. MakeGenericType closes it at run time — the pattern behind open-generic dependency injection registration. Closed types are what you use at compile time with List<SessionDto>.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying static fields on Generic<T> are shared across all T — Counter<int> and Counter<string> are independent. Confusing open and closed: you cannot instantiate List<> without a type argument. Claiming generic methods always need explicit type args — inference works from parameters unless T is return-only. Strong answer: open vs closed, statics per closed type, generic sharing for reference T, inference rules.

interviewTakeaways: Open generic List<> versus closed List<string>; static state is per closed type, not per open T.
Generic methods infer type arguments from call arguments; specify T explicitly when inference fails.
Generic sharing: reference-type type arguments often share JIT code; value types specialize per closure.

60s: Open generic has unbound T — typeof(List<>). Closed generic is List<string>. Statics are per closed type. Generic sharing applies to reference type args. Inference from call args unless T is return-only.
Follow-up: how does open-generic DI registration work with typeof(IHandler<>)?
commonPitfalls: Assuming static fields on Generic<T> are shared across all T — that gets rejected; Counter<int> and Counter<string> are separate.
Strong answer: static members belong to the closed constructed type, not the open generic definition.
Fighting inference instead of writing Foo<T>(...) explicitly when T appears only in the return type.
Confusing open generic typeof(List<>) with trying to new List<>() without a type argument.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript infers type arguments similarly from call arguments. There is no per-T static field at run time because generic parameters erase.

jsTsCorrelations.concept: no open generic at run time
jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has no typeof(List<>) equivalent. Open generic registration patterns in .NET DI have no direct JS analogue — you register concrete constructors.
